messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 22
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Product Manager
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 36

The first thing he tells me, settling into the chair with a practiced ease that doesn’t quite reach his eyes, is that he’s a product manager. He says it like a shield. He’s good at it, he explains—at managing timelines, deliverables, and the expectations of stakeholders. He’s been at the same tech startup for two years, promoted twice. He likes the structure. He likes that a problem, presented correctly, has a solution.

He was born in a small city in the north of Colombia. His family moved to the United States when he was seven, and he has few memories of the place. What he remembers is the heat, the sound of his grandmother’s voice, and the way his mother would check the locks on the doors three times before bed. That last part, he says, he always thought was just a habit. A quirk.

In June, he went back for the first time. His grandmother was ill, and his mother couldn’t get the time off work, so he went. He was there for nine days. He tells me about the first eight days in a flat, efficient tone—the food, the cousins he’d only ever seen in photographs, the way the city had changed. It was good, he says. Hard, but good.

On the ninth day, he was in a market with his aunt. He was looking at a stall that sold woven bags, thinking about which one to bring back for his mother. He heard a sound he still cannot fully describe. He says it was like the air itself tore open. He remembers being on the ground, his cheek pressed against the hot concrete, dust filling his mouth. He remembers his aunt’s hand on his back, pushing him down, her body covering his. He remembers the ringing in his ears, and then the screaming.

The bomb had detonated two blocks away. He was not injured. He was not even close to the epicenter. But something in him, he says, was detonated too.

That was four months ago.

Now, he sits in my office and tells me he is fine. He is not fine. His PCL-5 score is a 36, a number he doesn’t know and I do not share. He does not need a number to know that his life has become unmanageable.

He has stopped going to the office. He works from his apartment now, the blinds always drawn. He says it’s because the open-plan layout is distracting, but the real reason is that he cannot have anyone behind him. He has rearranged his desk so his back is to the wall. He has done the same with his bed. He checks the locks on his door three times before he sleeps, and he thinks about his mother, and he hates himself for the thought.

The triggers are everywhere and nowhere. A car backfiring on the street sends him to the floor of his kitchen, heart hammering, waiting for the second blast. A sudden, loud laugh in a coffee shop makes his vision go white. He has stopped going to coffee shops. He has stopped going anywhere with more than ten people. He canceled a product launch meeting last week because the conference room had no windows.

He dreams about the concrete. He dreams about the dust. He dreams about his aunt’s hand, but in the dream, it is not pressing him down to protect him. In the dream, it is pushing him under the ground.

He tells me all of this with a calm, clinical detachment, as if he is reporting on a project that has gone off the rails. He is not crying. He is not shaking. He is just describing the ruins, piece by piece, as if he has already accepted that this is where he lives now. He is a young man who went home to say goodbye to his grandmother, and he brought something back with him that he cannot name, cannot manage, and cannot return.
